title: Celsus names no shameful passage
source_text: Οἴεται δὲ καὶ τοὺς ἀπὸ τῶν προφητῶν ἀπολογουμένους περὶ τῶν κατὰ τὸν Χριστὸν μηδὲν μὲν δύνασθαι πρὸς ἔπος λέγειν, ἐπὰν φαίνηταί τι πονηρὸν ἢ αἰσχρὸν ἢ ἀκάθαρτον λεγόμενον περὶ τοῦ θείου ἢ μιαρόν. διὸ καὶ ὡς μηδεμιᾶς οὔσης ἀπολογίας συνείρει ἑαυτῷ μυρία περὶ τῶν μὴ διδομένων. εἰδέναι (δὲ) χρὴ ὅτι καὶ οἱ βουλόμενοι κατὰ τὰς θείας ζῆς γραφὰς καὶ ἐπιστάμενοι ὅτι „γνῶσις ἀσυνέτου ἀδιεξέταστοι λόγοι“ καὶ ἀναγνόντες τὸ „ἕτοιμοι ἀεὶ πρὸς ἀπολογίαν παντὶ τῷ αἰτοῦντι ἡμᾶς λόγου περὶ τῆς ἐν ἡμῖν ἐλπίδος“ οὐκ ἐπὶ μόνον τὸ προειρῆσθαι τάδε τινὰ καταφεύγουσιν, ἀλλὰ γὰρ καὶ τὰς δοκούσας ἀπεμφάσεις λύειν πειρῶνται καὶ δεικνύναι οὐδὲν εἶναι πονηρὸν ἐν τοῖς λόγοις οὐδ᾿ αἰσχρὸν οὐδ᾿ ἀκάθαρτον οὐδὲ μιαρὸν ἀλλὰ τοιοῦτον γίνεσθαι, ὡς χρὴ ἐκδέχεσθαι τοῖς μὴ συνιεῖσι τῆν θείαν γραφήν. ἐχρῆν δ᾿ αὐτὸν ἀπὸ τῶν προφητῶν τὸ φαινόμενον ἐν αὐτοῖς πονηρὸν ἢ τὸ δοκοῦν αὐτῷ αἰσχρὸν ἢ τὸ νομιζόμενον αὐτῷ ἀκάθαρτον ἢ ὃ ὑπελάμβανεν εἶναι μιαρὸν παραθέσθαι, εἴπερ τοιαῦτα ἔβλεπεν ἐν τοῖς προφήταις εἰρημένα· πληκτικώτερος γὰρ ἂν ὁ λόγος αὐτοῦ ἦν καὶ πρὸς ὃ ἐβούλετο ἀνυτικώτερος· νυνὶ δὲ οὐ παρέθετο, ἀλλ᾿ ἐπανατεινάμενος ἀπειλεῖ τοιαῦτα φαίνεσθαι ἐν ταῖς γραφαῖς, καταψευδόμενος αὐτῶν. πρὸς οὖν κενοὺς ψόφους ὀνομάτων οὐδεὶς λόγος αἱρεῖ ἀπολογήσασθαι ὑπὲρ τοῦ δεῖξαι ὅτι οὐδὲν πονηρὸν ἢ αἰσχρὸν ἢ ἀκάθαρτον ἢ μιαρόν ἐστιν ἐν τοῖς τῶν προφητῶν λόγοις.
pass_a_gloss: He supposes (οἴομαι) also that those who make a defence (ἀπολογέομαι) from the prophets about the things concerning Christ can say nothing to the point (πρὸς ἔπος), whenever something appears (φαίνομαι) being said about the divine (τὸ θεῖον) wicked (πονηρός) or shameful (αἰσχρός) or unclean (ἀκάθαρτος) or foul (μιαρός). Therefore also, as though there were no defence (ἀπολογία), he strings together (συνείρω) for himself countless things about things not granted (δίδωμι). (But) one must know that those who wish to live according to the divine Scriptures (θεῖαι γραφαί), and who know that [quotation] 'knowledge (γνῶσις) of the senseless (ἀσύνετος) is unexamined (ἀδιεξέταστος) words', and who have read the [quotation] 'ready (ἕτοιμος) always for a defence to everyone who asks us an account (λόγος) about the hope (ἐλπίς) in us', do not flee for refuge (καταφεύγω) to this alone, that these things were foretold, but also try to resolve (λύω) the seeming incongruities (ἀπέμφασις) and to show that there is nothing wicked in the words, nor shameful, nor unclean, nor foul, but that it becomes such, as one must interpret (ἐκδέχομαι), for those who do not understand (συνίημι) the divine Scripture. He ought to have set beside (παρατίθημι) from the prophets the thing appearing wicked in them, or the thing seeming to him shameful, or the thing thought (νομίζω) by him unclean, or what he supposed (ὑπολαμβάνω) to be foul, if indeed he saw such things said in the prophets; for his word would have been more striking (πληκτικός) and more effective (ἀνυτικός) toward what he wanted; but as it is he did not set [them] beside, but holding out (ἐπανατείνομαι) he threatens (ἀπειλέω) that such things appear in the Scriptures, lying against (καταψεύδομαι) them. Toward empty (κενός) noises (ψόφος) of names (ὄνομα), then, no reason (λόγος) proves [the need] to make a defence for showing that there is nothing wicked or shameful or unclean or foul in the words of the prophets.
pass_b_english: He also thinks that those who use the prophets to defend what concerns Christ can say nothing to the point whenever something wicked, shameful, unclean or foul appears to be said about the Deity. So, as though no defence existed, he strings together countless arguments for himself on points that are not granted.

But it must be understood that those who wish to live by the divine Scriptures, who know that “the knowledge of the senseless is unexamined words” (Sirach 21:18), and who have read the words “always ready to make a defence to everyone who asks us for an account of the hope that is in us” (1 Peter 3:15), do not take refuge only in the fact that these things were foretold. They also try to resolve the apparent incongruities, and to show that there is nothing wicked, shameful, unclean or foul in the words, but that they become so for those who do not understand the divine Scripture as it ought to be interpreted.

He ought to have set out from the prophets what appears wicked in them, or what seemed shameful to him, or what he thought unclean, or what he took to be foul, if he really saw such things said in the prophets; for his argument would then have struck harder and done more to achieve what he wanted. As it is, he set nothing out, but with a threatening flourish he declares that such things appear in the Scriptures, and in this he lies about them. No reason, then, requires a defence against mere empty noises of words, to show that there is nothing wicked, shameful, unclean or foul in the words of the prophets.

choices.choice: No words of Celsus are quoted directly; his four terms (wicked, shameful, unclean, foul) come through Origen’s report and are left unquoted. Copy-text: ζῆς is read as ζῆν (‘to live’); (δέ) is an editorial supplement. Sirach 21:18 is quoted exactly as in the Septuagint (γνῶσις ἀσυνέτου ἀδιεξέταστοι λόγοι). 1 Peter 3:15 is quoted with ἡμᾶς/ἡμῖν (‘us’) where the received text has ὑμᾶς/ὑμῖν (‘you’), and λόγου for λόγον; the English follows Origen. The clause ὡς χρὴ ἐκδέχεσθαι is taken with ‘understand’ (‘as it ought to be interpreted’). τὸ θεῖον rendered ‘the Deity’ (God, capitalised). συνείρει ἑαυτῷ μυρία περὶ τῶν μὴ διδομένων rendered ‘strings together countless arguments for himself on points that are not granted’; ‘arguments’ is supplied for μυρία. ἐπανατεινάμενος ἀπειλεῖ rendered ‘with a threatening flourish he declares’. κενοὺς ψόφους ὀνομάτων rendered ‘mere empty noises of words’. καταψευδόμενος αὐτῶν rendered ‘and in this he lies about them’.
τοὺς ἀπὸ τῶν προφητῶν ἀπολογουμένους: 'those who use the prophets to defend' instead of the stiff 'those who defend from the prophets'
Sirach 21:18: 'the knowledge of the senseless is unexamined words' (ἀσύνετος = senseless; natural word order)
καταψευδόμενος αὐτῶν: 'and in this he lies about them' instead of 'telling lies against them'
last sentence recast: 'No reason, then, requires a defence against mere empty noises of words' (οὐδεὶς λόγος αἱρεῖ kept as the subject)
Scripture checked: Sirach 21:18 and 1 Peter 3:15 confirmed

anf_compare.notes: Crombie (ANF 1872) and Chadwick (1953) were not used or consulted; the English is from the Greek.
